pr_title: Limit the task run per EventLoop tick via a timeout
pr_body:
Motivation:

We should better allow to limit the number of tasks that are run per EventLoop tick via a timeout. This timeout can be adjusted by -Dio.netty.eventLoop.maxTaskProcessingQuantumMs

Modifications:

Change property name and set default to 1 second.

Result:

Fixes https://github.com/netty/netty/issues/14165
pr_comments:
I have another question. 
Should we use the `final` to modify the maxTaskDurationPerRun field? 

Perhaps we could provide a `setMaxTaskDurationPerRun` method to allow users to adjust the configuration of their ioEventLoop?

> I have another question. Should we use the `final` to modify the maxTaskDurationPerRun field?
> 
> Perhaps we could provide a `setMaxTaskDurationPerRun` method to allow users to adjust the configuration of their ioEventLoop?

If we want we can add a constructor parameter for it... But I wanted to keep it simple for now.

issue_context.title: Can we make SingleThreadIoEventLoop ioRate configurable?
issue_context.body: Hi, I have 2 questions about SingleThreadIoEventLoop. 1. runAllTasks acept a nano timeout to decide how many time it can take to hanlde tasks. but now we're passing in a number of task to run. I think this may be a misusing. 2. Now we remove the ioRatio, and relate to 1st question, now we runIO once and then runAllTasks, but runAllTasks checks every 64 tasks. So if we're not running out of tasks, and asuming every task takes more than 1 nano, we will always have a fixed 1:64 ioRatio. can we bring back the ioRatio logic like before? I think we can record a time perid before and after runIO, and we can achieve same ioRatio control like before? ### Netty version 4.2.0.Alpha2
comments:
The implementation of the runAllTasks method contains an error, so I have prepared a draft Pull Request to fix it.
https://github.com/netty/netty/pull/14542。 
Please review it to check if I have fixed this misuse @normanmaurer 

About the ioRatio, I think that the IoEventLoop doesn't know what the IoHandler does. In the io_uring transport, handling I/O events is likely to consume less time compared to other transport implementations. so I think there is little reason to maintain the same ioRatio control as before.

It's my point of view, for your reference.

review_comments:
Yeah, in CFS this should be the target latency within a process should get its guaranteed fair schedule/chance to run IIRC.
And here, have a similarish meaning i.e. I/O will get its chance to run after this, although with a delay (our tasks are not preemptive).

TBH what CFS does is to update via a timer (the OS tick rate) the virtual time of the task running on CPU, guaranteed a min granularity time to run on the CPU or eventually perform a different decision if there are more.
